content: {"id": "9d5dbc2f-a229-4e2b-b65f-4586bf5c0348", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "What is the difference between an Application Load Balancer and a Network Load Balancer?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
{"id": "92e52826-56fa-4a03-96b8-7a23c070a802", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "chat_title", "title": "Application vs Network Load Balancer Differences Explained"}]}

{"id": "fe0135e0-ff57-4d48-bb06-defec7bc770d", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "thinking", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "This is a general AWS conceptual question rather than something about the DevOps Agent product itself, so I can just answer it directly with well-known information, no tool calls needed.\n\n"}]}

{"id": "b5e2cf5b-36fd-46fa-aa8f-4c62c2f41222", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Both distribute traffic across targets. The main difference is the network layer each one works at.

| | Application Load Balancer (ALB) | Network Load Balancer (NLB) |
|---|---|---|
| **OSI layer** | Layer 7 (application) | Layer 4 (transport) |
| **Protocols** | HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, WebSocket | TCP, UDP, TLS, TCP_UDP |
| **Routing** | Content-based. It routes on path, host header, HTTP headers, query strings, methods and source IP. | Connection-based. It routes on IP, port and protocol. |
| **Performance** | Good for web workloads. Latency is higher because it inspects requests. | Very high throughput and ultra-low latency. It handles millions of requests per second and sudden traffic spikes. |
| **IP addresses** | Dynamic. You use its DNS name. | One static IP per AZ, and you can attach Elastic IPs. It can also use private static IPs. |
| **Targets** | Instances, IPs, Lambda functions | Instances, IPs, and ALBs (an NLB can front an ALB) |
| **Security groups** | Supported | Supported (added in 2023). Older NLBs may not have them. |
| **TLS** | Terminates TLS and supports SNI. It can authenticate users with Cognito or OIDC. | Can terminate TLS, or pass TCP through untouched, so the target sees the encrypted traffic. |
| **Client IP** | Passed in the `X-Forwarded-For` header | Preserved as the source IP for instance targets |
| **Other features** | Redirects, fixed responses, weighted target groups, sticky sessions, WAF integration | PrivateLink (endpoint services), cross-zone balancing (off by default) |

**Choose an ALB when:**
- You run HTTP/HTTPS apps, microservices or containers.
- You need path-based or host-based routing, such as `/api` to one service and `/web` to another.
- You want WAF, authentication, redirects, or Lambda as a target.

**Choose an NLB when:**
- You need extreme performance or low latency.
- You use non-HTTP protocols such as TCP or UDP, for example gaming, IoT, VoIP, or databases.
- You need static or Elastic IPs, for example so clients can allowlist them.
- You want to expose a service through AWS PrivateLink.
- You want to pass TLS through to the backend unchanged.

A common pattern is to put an NLB in front of an ALB. That gives you static IPs and PrivateLink support from the NLB, plus Layer 7 routing from the ALB.

I can look at the load balancers in your account if you want. For example, I could check which ones you have and how they're configured.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
